topic: 限时写作：原因、办法与双边讨论
grammarFocus: 因果关系、条件和对比；段落间逻辑与指代。
title: The Repair Café: Causes, Solutions and Two Sides of a Community Project
instructions: 本材料为模拟英语听力练习，共四个部分，每部分10题，合计40题。所有场景、人名、数据均为原创模拟内容，不是官方雅思试题，也不对应任何官方分数。题型包括单选、填空和True/False/Not Given（三选一）。填空题答案必须与录音原文完全一致，且不超过字数限制。请先听录音（或阅读transcript），再作答。所有解析为中文，evidence为原文英文原句。
transcript:
Section 1: Social Dialogue

Woman: Hi, Tom. You look tired. Is everything all right?
Man: Not really, Mei. I'm helping to organise the Riverside Repair Café this Saturday, and we've hit a problem.
Woman: A repair café? What's that exactly?
Man: It's a free monthly event where volunteers fix broken things for local people — kettles, lamps, bicycles, that sort of thing. The idea is to stop people throwing away items that could easily be repaired.
Woman: That sounds lovely. So what's the problem?
Man: Well, we usually run it in the community hall, but the hall is being painted this month, so we've had to move to the old bus station on Mill Road.
Woman: The bus station? Is that big enough?
Man: It's actually bigger, which is good, but it's cold and there are only two power sockets. Last time we had eight volunteers with tools plugged in at the same time.
Woman: That's a real issue. Have you asked the council for help?
Man: I did, and they said they could lend us four extension cables, but we'd have to collect them ourselves before Friday.
Woman: That's manageable. What about the volunteers? Do you have enough people?
Man: We have six confirmed, but we need at least ten. Two of our regulars, Priya and her brother, cancelled because Priya has an exam on Monday.
Woman: I see. Could I help? I'm not good with electronics, but I can sew.
Man: Really? That would be perfect. We've had lots of requests about torn clothes and broken zips, and nobody on the team can sew.
Woman: Then I'll come. What time should I arrive?
Man: The café opens to the public at ten, but volunteers should be there at half past nine to set up the tables.
Woman: Half past nine. Got it. Should I bring my own sewing machine?
Man: If you don't mind. Ours is broken, which is a bit embarrassing for a repair café.
Woman: Ha! All right, I'll bring mine. And what about refreshments? Do you sell tea and cake?
Man: We do, and the money goes towards buying spare parts. But we've had a complaint that there's nothing for people who can't eat sugar, so this month we're adding fruit and some sugar-free biscuits.
Woman: Good idea. One more thing — how do people book a repair slot?
Man: They don't need to book. They just turn up with their item and wait. But we ask them to arrive before midday, because we stop accepting new items at twelve so the volunteers can finish by two.
Woman: That makes sense. I'll see you on Saturday, then.
Man: Thanks, Mei. You've really saved us.

Section 2: Social Monologue

Hello, this is Daniel Wu from the Northgate Community Trust with the monthly update. First, some good news. Our Repair Café project has now been running for one year, and in that time volunteers have fixed more than four hundred items. That means roughly four hundred objects that did not go to landfill. The most common repairs were lamps, kettles and small pieces of furniture.

Now, the reason I'm recording this message is that we need more volunteers, especially people who understand bicycles and sewing machines. We currently have eighteen volunteers, but only three of them can repair a bicycle, and demand for bike repairs has doubled since the spring.

We are also changing the day. From next month, the café will run on the first Sunday of each month instead of the first Saturday. The reason is simple: many of our volunteers work on Saturdays, and Sunday afternoons suit them better. The time stays the same, from ten in the morning until two in the afternoon.

A few practical points. Please do not bring microwaves. We had two last month, and our insurance does not cover microwave repairs because of the high-voltage parts inside. Also, if your item needs a spare part that we don't have, we will keep it for up to two weeks while we order the part, but after two weeks you must collect it, because we simply don't have the storage space.

Finally, a word about money. The project is free for users, but it costs about sixty pounds a month to run, mainly for spare parts and insurance. We are grateful to the local hardware shop, which donates screws, glue and paint. If you would like to help, you can put a donation in the box by the door, or you can join our volunteer team. Either way, thank you for listening, and I hope to see you on the first Sunday of next month.

Section 3: Academic Discussion

Tutor: All right, everyone. Today we're discussing the Riverside Repair Café case study. Let's start with causes. Why do you think repair cafés have become popular in the last ten years?
Student A: I'd say the main cause is the cost of living. If a kettle costs fifteen pounds and a repair is free, people will choose the repair.
Tutor: Good. Anyone want to add a cause?
Student B: Environmental concern. People are more aware of waste now. When an item goes to landfill, it causes pollution, so fixing it prevents that.
Tutor: Yes. And there's a third cause, which is social. These events bring neighbours together. Now, let's think about solutions. The Riverside café had a problem with power sockets. How did they solve it?
Student A: The council lent them extension cables. But that's only a short-term solution. A long-term solution would be to install more sockets in the building.
Tutor: Exactly — you've made an important distinction between short-term and long-term solutions. Now, some people argue that repair cafés are just a fashion and will disappear. What's your view?
Student B: I disagree, because the underlying causes — expensive goods and concern about waste — are not going away. However, I do think they depend on volunteers, and that's a weakness.
Student A: I agree with the first part but not the second. In my view, the volunteer model is actually a strength, because it builds community trust. If people feel involved, they keep coming back.
Tutor: Interesting — so you two disagree about whether volunteering is a weakness or a strength. Let's test that. What evidence would support Student B's view?
Student A: Well, the Northgate group lost two volunteers because of an exam, and they still can't find enough bike repairers. That suggests the model is fragile.
Tutor: Good. And what would support your view, that volunteering is a strength?
Student A: The fact that the hardware shop donates materials for free. That's a local business choosing to support the project, which shows trust.
Tutor: Nicely argued. One more point before we finish. How could we measure whether a repair café is successful?
Student B: We could count the number of items repaired. But that only measures one thing.
Tutor: Right. What else?
Student B: We could also measure how many people come back as volunteers, or how much waste is avoided. If we only count repairs, we might miss the social benefits.
Tutor: Excellent. So remember: when you write about a project like this, define your measure of success clearly, and support your claim with evidence from the case.

Section 4: Academic Lecture

Good morning. Today I want to look at why community repair projects succeed or fail, and I'll use the Riverside and Northgate examples throughout. There are three common causes of failure, and I'll deal with each in turn.

The first cause is what I call the skills gap. A repair café needs a mix of skills — electrical, mechanical, textile — and if one skill is missing, demand builds up in that area. At Northgate, bicycle repairs doubled in demand, yet only three of eighteen volunteers could repair a bicycle. Consequently, waiting times grew, and some users stopped coming. The solution is not simply to recruit more volunteers; it is to recruit for the missing skill. So the cause and the solution are directly linked.

The second cause is space and equipment. Many projects begin in borrowed rooms, and borrowed rooms come with limits. Riverside had only two power sockets, which restricted how many volunteers could work at once. Notice that the council's extension cables solved the immediate problem, but they did not solve the underlying one. If a project relies on temporary equipment, it remains fragile. A more durable solution is a written agreement with the building's owner that guarantees access to power and storage.

The third cause is money, but not in the way you might expect. Repair cafés are cheap to run — Northgate spends about sixty pounds a month — yet they are not free. Insurance, spare parts and heating all cost something. The danger is that a project assumes it is free and therefore never plans its finances. A simple solution is a small regular donation system, combined with partnerships, such as the hardware shop that donates materials. Partnerships reduce costs, and they also create a sense of shared ownership.

Now, let me turn to the two-sided debate. Supporters argue that repair cafés reduce waste, save money and build community. Critics argue three things. First, they say the environmental benefit is small, because the items repaired are few compared with total consumption. Second, they claim that repairs are often low quality and the item breaks again. Third, they warn that free repair may discourage people from buying better-quality goods in the first place.

How should we weigh these views? I'd suggest three criteria. First, scale: four hundred items a year is small nationally but significant locally. Second, durability: if a repaired kettle lasts another two years, the benefit is real. Third, additionality: does the café create benefits that would not exist otherwise, such as skills and social contact? On all three criteria, the evidence is mixed but broadly positive. Therefore, my conclusion is not that repair cafés will replace recycling, but that they work best as part of a wider strategy — alongside better product design, clearer labelling and, above all, local participation.
